text: Just past the top of the ridge, David ran into Ziba, Mephibosheth's servant, who had brought a pair of loaded donkeys carrying bread, raisin cakes, summer fruit, and a skin of wine.

The king asked what all this was for, and Ziba explained that the donkeys were for the royal household to ride, the food was for the young men to eat, and the wine was for anyone who grew faint out in the wilderness.

David then asked where his master's grandson was, and Ziba answered that Mephibosheth had stayed behind in Jerusalem, expecting that the house of Israel would restore his grandfather's kingdom to him.
So the king told Ziba that everything that had belonged to Mephibosheth now belonged to him, and Ziba bowed and thanked him, asking only to keep finding favor in the king's eyes.
As King David reached Bahurim, a man from Saul's own family came out cursing him without stopping — his name was Shimei, son of Gera.
He threw stones at David and at all his officials, even though the king's soldiers and mighty men surrounded him on both sides.
Shimei shouted as he cursed, telling David to get out, calling him a murderer and a worthless man.
He said the LORD was paying David back for all the blood of Saul's family, whose throne he had taken, and had now handed the kingdom to his son Absalom instead, since David was a man of bloodshed.
Abishai, Zeruiah's son, asked the king why this dead dog should be allowed to curse him, and asked for permission to go over and cut off his head.
But the king told Abishai and his brother to stay out of it — if the LORD had told the man to curse David, who could question it?
David added that if his own son was trying to kill him, it made sense that a Benjaminite might do the same; better to leave the man alone and let him curse, since the LORD had told him to.
Perhaps, David said, the LORD would notice the wrong being done to him and repay him with good in place of the curses he was receiving that day.
So David and his men kept walking along the road while Shimei matched their pace on the hillside across from them, cursing, throwing stones, and kicking up dust the whole way.
The king and everyone with him finally reached the Jordan, exhausted, and stopped there to rest and recover.
Meanwhile Absalom and the men of Israel arrived in Jerusalem, with Ahithophel accompanying him.
When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came before Absalom, he greeted him twice with, long live the king.
Absalom asked him whether this was how he showed loyalty to his friend, wondering why he hadn't gone with David instead.
Hushai answered that he would side with whoever the LORD, the people, and the men of Israel had chosen, and would stay with that man.
Besides, he said, who should he serve if not the son? Just as he had served the father, he would now serve him.
Then Absalom turned to Ahithophel and asked him for his advice on what to do next.

Ahithophel told him to go in to his father's concubines, left behind to look after the palace — once all Israel heard he had made himself utterly repugnant to his father, everyone following him would be emboldened.
So they set up a tent for Absalom on the roof, and he went in to his father's concubines where all Israel could see it.
In those days, the advice Ahithophel gave carried the weight of an oracle from God himself — that was how both David and Absalom regarded anything he counseled.
